standard.justification: The forms now standard already occur in Roman and medieval material, but stricter modern canonical order is typical chiefly in modern usage.

additive4.justification: Additive fours and nines are ordinary in the examined Roman and medieval records and survive in early modern accounts and modern clocks and monuments.

irregularSub.justification: Classical exceptions have narrow scope, and late-fifteenth-century IC is attested in print and stone; a wider period rating for IL or XM lacks equivalent evidence.

runSub.justification: Flavian IIX and XIIX, Republican XXC, and incunable iic/iiic belong to identifiable traditions, with scarce evidence in the intervening centuries.

oddOrder.justification: Individually documented exceptions such as classical XXCIII and reported eighth-century LXL support a low prior for named forms, conditional on structure and context.

additiveSum.justification: Certain lower-before-higher medieval ordinals are additive in Latin word order, but the general method of ignoring order is only a fallback.

multiplicative.justification: Raised C and M are frequent in some late medieval accounts and attested in sixteenth-century commercial arithmetic and Scottish records.

multiplicativePlain.justification: Baseline multiplication is reported sporadically for classical thousands and attested in later medieval and early modern evidence, sometimes with a separating dot or an abbreviated unit word.

vigesimal.justification: Score notation is reported as frequent in late-medieval print and characterises some French and British records, with continued use in early modern hands.

separate.justification: Final j marks a numeral in some hands, but an internal j alone lacks evidence as a rule for splitting adjacent values.

vinculum.justification: The Roman ×1,000 overbar and medieval continuation are documented, while an identical-looking stroke can mark a numeral or abbreviation.

frame.justification: Roman three-sided frames multiply by 100,000 in rare high-value inscriptions, with no independently dated examples of continued ordinary use in the other bins.

apostrophus.justification: Ancient inscriptional signs, Priscian's account around 500 and Renaissance imprints establish use and transmission; the evidence does not establish general popularity.

archaic.justification: The archaic fifty and the late six belong to different histories, with the latter particularly well evidenced in late Antiquity and early medieval hands.

ignored.justification: Units, date words, ordinal marks and abbreviations require recognition or warning; discarding unknown glyphs is a software fallback.

minim.justification: Similar strokes motivate alternative transcriptions in late medieval and early modern hands, with judgement required for the individual token.

ad.justification: The Christian era spreads in the early Middle Ages and becomes ordinary for years in later Western sources, with local differences in year start.

omittedMillennium.justification: A late-medieval León fragment is a candidate, but secure omission of the thousand alone remains unverified and other apparently similar cases spell out mille.

omittedCentury.justification: Pollard describes occasional shortening by late-fifteenth-century printers and documents XCij for 1492 in Augsburg.

auc.justification: The Hadrianic city date is secure and Renaissance humanists and modern scholarship use AUC retrospectively; require the era and epoch to be supplied.

chronogram.justification: Meaningful additive letter-dates have an especially well-documented early modern European tradition, distinct from an arbitrary sum of a dirty numeral.

medievalLetters.justification: Glossaries and specialised local traditions give differing values. A selected source profile is necessary.

regnalYear.justification: Regnal or office years require authority, jurisdiction and an accession rule, and continue in some forms after the Middle Ages.

indiction.justification: A 15-year cycle used by medieval chanceries and some later notaries narrows a dated interval when the year-start style is known.

spanishEra.justification: Iberian inscriptions and documents use an era counted from 38 BCE with regional end dates.

byzantineAnnoMundi.justification: Selected Byzantine manuscript dates use a world era whose year starts in September, so the month controls the conversion.

finalJ.justification: A long or descended last i is written j in many later Western hands and in fifteenth-century print.

ordinalMarks.justification: Raised ordinal endings such as o in date formulae may carry grammar while leaving the numeral value unchanged.

distinctionMarks.justification: Dots and strokes can distinguish numerals or currency from letters; they are evidence to retain even when they do not modify the value.

clockIIII.justification: Four strokes are the usual form on modern Roman-numeral dials in the cited synthesis, with older clock examples and surviving alternatives.

hybridNumerals.justification: Some late medieval and early modern examples mix number words, Arabic digits or special units with Roman numeral signs.

earlyFifty.justification: The early arrow-like forms of fifty are distinct from the late six and from L.

lateSix.justification: A late-form six appears from the imperial period and in late-antique and early medieval hands; specialised sources disagree on origins and the end of related forms.
